rules.statement: In a test project, don't ask to move a private sealed stub, fake or sample type that only one test file uses out of that file into its own top-level file: the test conventions require it to be nested there, and the no-nested-types rule covers production code only.
rules.why: The maintainer declined several findings: csharp-tests.instructions.md requires a one-file stub to be a private sealed nested type, and the no-nested-types rule in csharp-production.instructions.md applies only to src/**.
rules.check: Before reporting a nested type in test code, check whether more than one test file uses it. Report it only when two or more files share it.

rules.statement: In a test project, don't ask for test stubs duplicated across two test projects to be merged into one shared helper when no shared test library exists: each project keeps its own nested copy, trimmed to the members its tests need.
rules.why: There is no shared test project, and the test conventions nest a one-file stub in its own file, so each project keeps its own copy.
rules.check: Before reporting duplicated stubs, check whether the copies are in different test projects and whether a shared test library already exists that both reference.

rules.statement: In a test file, don't flag a `#region Scaffolding` that groups test helpers as a nonstandard region name: it is the established name for test helpers.
rules.why: 130 test files use `#region Scaffolding`, and the template's region list doesn't forbid a helpers region, so renaming it in one file would make that file inconsistent with the rest.
rules.check: Before reporting a region name in a test file, count how often sibling test files use the same name.

rules.statement: In a test, don't pass `null!` for an argument the code under test shouldn't read; pass a strict mock with no setups instead.
rules.why: `null!` suppresses the nullable check instead of fixing its cause. A strict mock with no setups also proves the code never reads the argument.
rules.check: Look for `null!` arguments in added test code.

rules.statement: In a test, narrow a nullable value with an assertion such as `Assert.NotNull` or `Assert.IsType<T>(..., exactMatch: false)` before dereferencing it, rather than using the null-forgiving operator.
rules.why: With `!`, a missing member fails with a NullReferenceException instead of a clear assertion failure.
rules.check: Look for `!` on indexer or member access, such as `json["x"]!`, in test code.

rules.statement: Give each strict-mock setup that the code under test must call `.Verifiable()`, and put the setup only in the tests that reach the call.
rules.why: Without `.Verifiable()`, no test fails if production code stops making the call.
rules.check: Look for strict-mock `Setup(...).Returns(...)` chains in added tests that don't end in `.Verifiable()`.

rules.statement: Keep the exact script or commands that generate an independent-oracle test fixture in a comment above the fixture's constants, and note there when the output is randomized.
rules.why: Without the script, the fixture can't be reproduced or audited.
rules.check: Look for hard-coded cryptographic test vectors whose comment describes how they were generated in prose but doesn't include the script or commands.

rules.statement: When validating configured or registered string codes, use `string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace`, and throw an InvalidOperationException that names the problem when a registration entry is null, rather than letting a NullReferenceException escape.
rules.why: A whitespace code registers an entry that nothing can look up, and startup gives no error naming the problem.
rules.check: Look for `string.IsNullOrEmpty` on identifiers or codes, and for registration loops that dereference entries without a null check.

rules.statement: When an error message rejects a value that must come from a known set, list the accepted values in the message.
rules.why: Otherwise an operator with a mistyped value has to look up the valid values elsewhere.
rules.check: Look for rejection messages for enum-like or registered values that name only the bad value.

rules.statement: Hold secret material such as a shared secret or a key-encryption key in a sensitive `BufferFactory.Rent(..., isSensitive: true, ...)` rental, including the fallback above the stackalloc limit, rather than in a pinned GC array that is wiped by hand.
rules.why: A pinned GC array keeps the secret outside the secure pool, and it is wiped only by a manual ZeroMemory call.
rules.check: Look for `GC.AllocateUninitializedArray<byte>(..., pinned: true)` or `new byte[]` that holds key material.

rules.statement: Use the framework's size constant, such as `SHA256.HashSizeInBytes`, instead of a literal like `256 >> 3` for a hash or block size.
rules.why: If the hash were ever changed, a literal size could silently disagree with it outside debug builds.
rules.check: Look for numeric literals or shifts used as digest sizes next to hash API calls.

rules.statement: Validate a key against a curve-bound algorithm by the key's actual curve, not by its type and size alone, and fail closed when the curve can't be determined.
rules.why: Two curves can share a size, so a key on the wrong curve could be accepted at declaration time and only fail later at runtime.
rules.check: Look for key/algorithm compatibility checks that compare only key type and bit size, or that skip the curve check when the curve is unknown.

rules.statement: Give a rule shared by several code paths, such as choosing a key's curve or reading a stored public key with its exception filter, one shared implementation, and return its result to the callers so they can't skip it, rather than copying the logic into each class.
rules.why: Copies drift. Different paths could then choose different curves, or let an exception escape as a 500 on one path and not on another.
rules.check: Look for the same lookup, resolution or try/catch logic duplicated across classes, especially with different exception filters.

rules.statement: In decision records and CHANGELOG entries, state the current behaviour in the present tense, and don't add amendments, deltas or breaking notes that only record how a pull request's own drafts evolved.
rules.why: Notes about intermediate drafts contradict the record's other statements and mislead readers.
rules.check: Look for amendment notes, 'now' or 'no longer' deltas, or Breaking entries that describe changes made earlier in the same unreleased work.

rules.statement: Name a buffer or field for what it actually holds, and give overloads with different roles different names.
rules.why: Misleading names make code harder to audit, and they make it easy to confuse which overload does what.
rules.check: Look for buffers reused for unrelated outputs, locals with numeric suffixes such as `x2`, and same-named overloads with different responsibilities.
